newsitem.title: USA: "Lost gospel" find meets mixed U.S. reaction.
newsitem.headline: "Lost gospel" find meets mixed U.S. reaction.

text.p: U.S. bible scholars reacted with a mixture of scepticism and curiosity on Friday to claims by two U.S. academics that they have identified a "lost gospel" containing dialogue between Jesus Christ and his disciples.

Two U.S. religious studies professors, Paul Mirecki and Charles Hedrick, said earlier this week they believe the fragmented text is an early account of Jesus' teachings and probably originated with one of several first or second-century Christian minority groups known as Gnostics.

Marvin Meyer, professor of religion at Chapman University in California and an expert in so-called Gnostic gospels, said the text was "a very exciting find" because it may provide more insight into the early days of Christianity.
"A text like this will give us more perspective on how early Christians believed and thought about things, including how they believed and thought about Jesus," Meyer said.

He said the text may also add to information contained in the four New Testament Gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, thereby giving scholars a clearer picture of the historical figure known as Jesus of Nazareth.

Mirecki said the badly damaged manuscript, written in an ancient Egyptian language called Coptic, was probably a fourth- or fifth-century translation of an earlier Gnostic document. The term Gnostic applies to dozens of groups that broke with orthodox Christianity by believing that they were privy to secret knowledge that was essential to salvation.

David Scholer, professor of New Testament at Fuller Theological Seminary in California and Mirecki's former professor, said that while the text could shed light on early Christianity, it was unlikely that it would provide any reliable information about the life of Jesus Christ.

"This manuscript would certainly add to our knowledge of... diversity in second-century Christianity and the growth of what we call the Gnostic phenomenon," Scholer said. "But... given its obvious Gnostic character and its similarity to other such texts, whether it preserves any data about the historical Jesus can never be known."

Anthony Tambasco, chair of the Theology Department at Georgetown University, echoed Scholer's views. "It's certainly not going to be one of those things where we discovered a new gospel and it's going to force us to rewrite Christianity," he said.

Mirecki and Hedrick found the fourth- or fifth-century manuscript in 1991 in Berlin's Egyptian Museum, but it took them until recently to piece together the document's content. Scholer, who has not yet seen the manuscript, said he would want to know more details about where in Egypt the text was first discovered and how it wound up in the Berlin museum.

Donald Senior, professor of New Testament at Catholic Theological Union in Chicago, said that although he has not seen the text, he suspected the newly identified gospel probably reinterpreted the four New Testament Gospels and was not a unique account of Christ's life.
